days.title: Coupled Reactions & ATP
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Define coupled reactions.
  • Explain the role of ATP in energy coupling.
  • Describe ATP structure and hydrolysis.
  • Explain energy transfer in cells.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • ATP — adenosine triphosphate; the energy currency of the cell.
  • Energy coupling — using exergonic reactions to drive endergonic ones.
  • Exergonic — releases energy.
  • Endergonic — absorbs energy.

📚 Lesson Content

A. ATP Structure

ATP = adenine + ribose + 3 phosphate groups. The bonds between phosphate groups store energy.

B. ATP Hydrolysis

ATP + H₂O → ADP + Pi + Energy. This releases ~7.3 kcal/mol.

C. Energy Coupling

Cells use the energy from ATP hydrolysis to drive endergonic reactions (e.g., protein synthesis, active transport).

D. Coupled Reactions in Photosynthesis

Light reactions (exergonic, produce ATP/NADPH) are coupled to the Calvin cycle (endergonic, uses ATP/NADPH to build glucose).

💬 Let's Discuss

Living things are always doing work: muscles contract, pumps push ions, cells build proteins. Each of these needs energy, but the energy in food cannot be used directly. Cells first store it in a small, ready-to-spend molecule: ATP (adenosine triphosphate).

ATP is made of adenine (a base), ribose (a sugar) and three phosphate groups. The phosphates are all negatively charged and repel each other, like compressed springs. When the last phosphate is removed by adding water (hydrolysis), ATP becomes ADP + Pi and releases energy (about 7.3 kcal per mole). Cells then rebuild ATP from ADP and Pi using energy from food or sunlight. This ATP–ADP cycle is so fast that your body recycles roughly its own weight in ATP every day.

Reactions are of two types. Exergonic reactions release energy (breaking down glucose, hydrolyzing ATP) — think ex = exit. Endergonic reactions require energy (building proteins, pumping ions against a gradient) — en = enter. An endergonic reaction cannot happen alone. Cells link it to an exergonic one so that the energy released by one drives the other. This is energy coupling, and ATP is the go-between: respiration (exergonic) makes ATP, and ATP hydrolysis (exergonic) powers active transport or protein synthesis (endergonic). It works like money: you earn it in one place and spend it in another.

Photosynthesis also couples reactions: the light reactions make ATP and NADPH, which are then spent in the Calvin cycle to build sugar.

Common mistake: saying ATP "stores a lot of energy for a long time." It is short-term currency; long-term storage is fat and glycogen.

days.title: Pigments & Light Absorption
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the major features of photosynthesis.
  • Identify the pigments involved.
  • Explain light absorption and reflection.
  • Relate pigments to their roles.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Chlorophyll a — primary pigment; absorbs blue-violet and red.
  • Chlorophyll b — accessory pigment; absorbs blue and orange.
  • Carotenoids — accessory pigments; absorb blue-green; protect chlorophyll.
  • Action spectrum — wavelengths that drive photosynthesis.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Photosynthesis Overview

6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂

Occurs in chloroplasts. Two stages: light reactions (thylakoid) and Calvin cycle (stroma).

B. Pigments

PigmentAbsorbsRole
Chlorophyll aBlue-violet, redPrimary pigment
Chlorophyll bBlue, orangeAccessory pigment
CarotenoidsBlue-greenAccessory + photoprotection

C. Why Leaves Are Green

Chlorophyll reflects green light — that's why we see leaves as green.

💬 Let's Discuss

Sunlight looks white, but it is a mix of colors, each with a different wavelength. Pigments are molecules that absorb certain wavelengths and reflect others; the color we see is the reflected light. Chlorophyll absorbs mostly blue-violet and red light and reflects green — that is why leaves look green.

Chlorophyll a is the primary pigment; it is the only one that directly passes energized electrons into the light reactions. Chlorophyll b and the carotenoids (yellow, orange — carotene and xanthophyll) are accessory pigments. They absorb wavelengths chlorophyll a misses and pass the energy on, widening the range of usable light. Carotenoids also protect chlorophyll from damage by too much light. In tropical trees and in mango or talisay leaves turning yellow-orange as they age, chlorophyll breaks down first and the carotenoids that were always there become visible.

A graph of how much light each pigment absorbs is its absorption spectrum. A graph of how fast photosynthesis runs at each wavelength is the action spectrum. They match closely, with peaks in blue and red and a dip in green — evidence that these pigments drive photosynthesis.

Photosynthesis happens in two linked stages inside the chloroplast: the light reactions in the thylakoid membranes (where the pigments are) and the Calvin cycle in the stroma. Overall: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.

Common mistake: "Leaves are green because chlorophyll absorbs green light." It is the opposite: green is the color it reflects, and uses least.

days.title: Light Reactions — Electron Flow
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the light reactions.
  • Trace the path of electrons.
  • Explain photosystems I and II.
  • Describe ATP and NADPH production.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Photosystem II (PSII) — splits water; produces O₂.
  • Photosystem I (PSI) — produces NADPH.
  • Electron transport chain (ETC) — passes electrons between photosystems.
  • Chemiosmosis — ATP production via H⁺ gradient.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Path of Electrons

  1. Light excites electrons in PSII
  2. Water is split to replace electrons (O₂ released)
  3. Electrons travel down ETC, pumping H⁺ into thylakoid
  4. Electrons reach PSI and are re-excited
  5. Electrons reduce NADP⁺ to NADPH
  6. H⁺ flows back through ATP synthase → ATP produced

B. Products of Light Reactions

  • ATP — energy for Calvin cycle
  • NADPH — reducing power for Calvin cycle
  • O₂ — released as byproduct

💬 Let's Discuss

The light reactions turn light energy into chemical energy in two forms: ATP and NADPH. They happen in the thylakoid membranes, where pigments are grouped into two photosystems. Confusingly, Photosystem II acts first — it was simply discovered second.

1. Photosystem II: light excites electrons in chlorophyll a, and they jump to a carrier. To replace them, PSII splits water (photolysis): 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂. This is where all the oxygen we breathe comes from — the water, not the CO₂. 2. Electron transport chain: the excited electrons pass down a chain of carriers to Photosystem I. The energy they lose is used to pump H⁺ ions into the thylakoid space. 3. Photosystem I: light re-energizes the electrons, and they are finally handed to NADP⁺, making NADPH. 4. Chemiosmosis: H⁺ ions, now crowded inside the thylakoid, flow back out through ATP synthase, which makes ATP.

So, inputs: light, water, ADP, NADP⁺. Outputs: ATP, NADPH and O₂. The ATP and NADPH do not stay; they move to the stroma to power the Calvin cycle, which returns ADP and NADP⁺ to be reused. Notice the similarity with respiration: both use an ETC, an H⁺ gradient and ATP synthase.

Common mistake: saying the light reactions make glucose. They make only ATP, NADPH and O₂; glucose is built in the Calvin cycle.

days.title: The Calvin Cycle
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the three phases of the Calvin cycle.
  • Explain carbon fixation.
  • Describe the role of RuBisCO.
  • Explain the products of the Calvin cycle.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Calvin cycle — light-independent reactions producing glucose.
  • Carbon fixation — attaching CO₂ to an organic molecule.
  • RuBisCO — the enzyme that fixes CO₂.
  • G3P — the product used to make glucose.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Three Phases

PhaseWhat Happens
1. Carbon fixationCO₂ + RuBP → 3-PGA (via RuBisCO)
2. Reduction3-PGA → G3P using ATP and NADPH
3. RegenerationRuBP is regenerated to continue the cycle

B. Products

  • For every 3 CO₂, 1 G3P is produced
  • Two G3P molecules → 1 glucose
  • ATP and NADPH from light reactions power the cycle

💬 Let's Discuss

The Calvin cycle takes place in the stroma and builds sugar from CO₂. It does not need light directly, which is why it is sometimes called the "light-independent reactions" — but it depends completely on the ATP and NADPH from the light reactions, so in practice it stops in the dark.

The cycle has three phases. 1. Carbon fixation: the enzyme RuBisCO attaches CO₂ from the air to a five-carbon sugar called RuBP. The unstable six-carbon product splits into two three-carbon molecules. RuBisCO is probably the most abundant protein on Earth, because it is slow and plants need a lot of it. 2. Reduction: ATP and NADPH are spent to convert those molecules into G3P (glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate), a three-carbon sugar. This is the redox step: NADPH donates electrons, reducing carbon. 3. Regeneration: most of the G3P is rearranged, using more ATP, to rebuild RuBP so the cycle can continue.

The bookkeeping: for every 3 CO₂ fixed, the cycle uses 9 ATP and 6 NADPH and releases 1 G3P. Two G3P molecules (from 6 turns) can be joined into one glucose. The plant then uses the sugar to make sucrose for transport, starch for storage and cellulose for walls — and to fuel its own respiration.

Every grain of rice you eat is carbon that RuBisCO once pulled from the air. Common mistake: saying the Calvin cycle releases O₂. Oxygen comes only from the light reactions.
